questions.stem: In the pre-admission clinic you are explaining Samuel's colonoscopy. He will have propofol sedation given by an anaesthetist. He says it is tax time, and asks whether he can drive himself home afterwards and get back to the office that afternoon. His partner Jess could collect him. What is the best advice?
options: He may drive once he is alert in recovery, usually 1 to 2 hours after the procedure ends
He can take a taxi home on his own and work from home that afternoon
Jess takes him home; no driving, alcohol, big decisions or legal documents for 24 hours
Jess takes him home, but he can go back to work that afternoon if he feels well
questions.why: Sedation dulls judgement and reaction time for longer than the patient feels it does. A responsible adult must take him home, ideally stay overnight, and he should not drive, drink alcohol, operate machinery, make important decisions or sign legal documents for 24 hours.
notes: Feeling alert in recovery does not mean the sedation has worn off, and driving is not allowed for 24 hours after sedation.
Going home alone in a taxi is not safe: a responsible adult needs to take him home, and work decisions should wait 24 hours.
Being driven home is right, but going back to work the same afternoon means making important decisions while still affected by sedation.

questions.stem: Samuel, 25, has ileocolonic Crohn's disease confirmed at colonoscopy: terminal ileal ulcers, a mildly narrowed ileocaecal valve and patchy right colonic ulcers. He is well enough to be managed as an outpatient. The gastroenterologist rates the activity as mild to moderate ileocaecal disease. Which treatment is first-line to induce remission?
options: Oral mesalazine 4 g daily in divided doses for 8 weeks, then reassess
Oral azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg daily as monotherapy, reviewed at 12 weeks
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly as an inpatient, then switch to oral prednisolone
Oral budesonide 9 mg daily for about 8 weeks, then taper
questions.why: Controlled-release budesonide releases the drug in the ileum and right colon. Most of it is broken down on first pass through the liver, so it has fewer systemic steroid effects. It is first-line induction for mild to moderate ileocaecal Crohn's disease, and is tapered once he responds.
notes: Mesalazine has little effect in Crohn's disease and is not recommended to induce remission, unlike in ulcerative colitis.
Thiopurines take about 3 months to work, so they are used for steroid-sparing maintenance, not on their own to induce remission.
IV corticosteroids are for acute severe disease needing admission, which a stable outpatient with mild to moderate disease does not have.

questions.stem: Samuel, 25, with active Crohn's disease (CRP 28), has Hb 118 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 16 µg/L and transferrin saturation 8% despite 3 weeks of oral iron. The gastroenterologist plans IV iron instead. Which mechanism best explains why oral iron works poorly while his bowel is inflamed?
options: Inflammation lowers hepcidin, so stored iron leaks from macrophages and is lost
The terminal ileum is the main site of iron absorption and it is ulcerated
Inflammation lowers gastric acid, so dietary ferric iron is not reduced to ferrous
IL-6 raises hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin and blocks enterocyte iron export
questions.why: Inflammatory cytokines, mainly IL-6, make the liver produce more hepcidin. Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, so iron stays trapped in enterocytes and macrophages and oral iron is poorly absorbed. This is why IV iron is preferred in active IBD.
notes: Inflammation raises hepcidin rather than lowering it, and the effect is to trap iron in macrophages, not to release it.
Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. The terminal ileum is where vitamin B12 and bile salts are absorbed.
Gastric acid is not the main problem in Crohn's disease, and Ferro-Grad is already ferrous iron, so no reduction step is needed.

questions.stem: Samuel's colonoscopy shows Crohn's disease in the distal 10 cm of the terminal ileum, with an ulcerated, mildly narrowed ileocaecal valve. If the narrowing progresses, he may later need an ileocaecal resection. Which artery is the main blood supply to this segment?
options: Middle colic artery, from the superior mesenteric artery
Ileocolic artery, from the superior mesenteric artery
Right colic artery, from the inferior mesenteric artery
Ileal arteries, from the coeliac trunk
questions.why: The ileocolic artery is the last branch on the right side of the superior mesenteric artery. It supplies the terminal ileum, the caecum and the appendix, and it is the vessel ligated in an ileocaecal resection.
notes: The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon, not the terminal ileum or caecum.
The right colic artery comes from the superior mesenteric artery, not the inferior mesenteric artery, and it supplies the ascending colon rather than the ileocaecal region.
Ileal arteries come from the superior mesenteric artery. The coeliac trunk supplies foregut structures such as the stomach, liver and proximal duodenum.
